passage: In Class 5 at the city school, Bhupen Sir held up Sabina's notebook so everyone could see. "Look at this mess. Is this what you call homework?" A few children laughed. Sabina's face burned and her eyes stung. She stared at her desk and wished the floor would open. She had stayed up late, but her pencil had smudged in the humid flat. At home she did not touch her dinner. When Papa asked, she told him. He listened, then said, "You did not deserve that in front of everyone." The next day he met Sabina's class teacher, who said she would talk with Bhupen Sir.

qa.q: What did Bhupen Sir hold up for everyone to see?
qa.a: He held up Sabina's notebook.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and wanted to disappear; her face burned and her eyes stung.

qa.q: What could Sabina do if a teacher scolds her in public again?
qa.a: She can tell a parent or another teacher what happened, as she did with her father, and remember the shame is not hers to carry.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt hearing what happened?
qa.a: Papa probably felt upset for his daughter and protective, which is why he told her she did not deserve it and went to meet her class teacher.

grounding: A child scolded in front of the whole class wants to vanish, tells her parent, and an adult follows up.

passage: The school office smelled of chalk and floor polish. Avni sat next to her mother while Kashish, her classmate, waited on the bench outside. That morning the teacher had made Avni stand in the corridor for spilling paint, though she had only picked up a bottle someone else knocked over. Avni's hands were damp. But she took a breath and told her mother everything, from the bottle to the corridor. Her mother listened without interrupting. "Thank you for telling me the whole story," she said. Later she spoke to the teacher, who checked with Kashish and cleared it up. Avni felt lighter.

qa.q: Where did the teacher make Avni stand?
qa.a: The teacher made her stand in the corridor.

qa.q: Why did Avni decide to tell her mother the whole story even with damp hands?
qa.a: She trusted her mother to listen and hoped the truth would be heard, though she was nervous.

qa.q: What made it easier for the truth to come out?
qa.a: Avni's full account and her mother's calm listening led the mother to speak to the teacher, who then checked with Kashish. 🙂

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt being asked by the teacher?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt nervous at first, having seen it happen, but could also have been glad to help clear things up for her classmate.

grounding: A child punished unfairly still tells her parent the whole story and finds that trusting them helps the truth come out.

passage:
"Didi, can I tell you something?" Damini said on the terrace.
"Of course," said Lalremsiami.
"Sir kept my drawing and gave me zero, and I did not even copy it. He said the decision is final."
"That sounds awful."
"I felt so helpless. He is the teacher, so I just stood there."
"You do not have to swallow that or get back at him. What if you ask him politely to look at it again?"
"He might say no."
"He might. But you will have said it."
"Will you come with me?"
"I will wait outside the staff room."
Damini breathed out slowly.

qa.q: What did Sir give Damini for the drawing?
qa.a: He kept Damini's drawing and gave it zero.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when saying "I just stood there"?
qa.a: Damini felt helpless because the teacher decided and Damini could not argue back.

qa.q: What could Damini do next to be heard without revenge?
qa.a: Damini can politely ask the teacher to look at the drawing again, with Lalremsiami waiting nearby for support.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Damini's polite request?
qa.a: The teacher may see a student who respects him but wants a fair look, and might reconsider, though he may also say no.

grounding: A child who cannot argue with an adult's decision names that helplessness to someone safe and plans to ask politely to be heard.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 4. On Monday Bharati was made to stay in during play for breaking the classroom clock, which she did not do. I believed it was true because the clock fell when I was out of the room. After school Raghav, her classmate from the same row, came to my desk with his bag on his shoulder, looking at the floor. He said quietly, "Sir, it was not Bharati. A ball hit it. I saw." He added that he was scared to say so. I thanked him and told him it took courage. Next morning I spoke to Bharati, apologised and asked the boys who threw the ball to own up. Hemant Sir.

qa.q: What was Bharati made to stay in for?
qa.a: She was made to stay in during play for breaking the classroom clock.

qa.q: What does Raghav's looking at the floor while he spoke suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was nervous and scared to speak up, though he wanted to help Bharati.

qa.q: What could Raghav do if a classmate is blamed unfairly again?
qa.a: He can quietly tell a teacher what he saw, as he did, and perhaps ask a friend to come with him if it feels too scary.

qa.q: How might Bharati have felt when Hemant Sir apologised?
qa.a: Bharati probably felt relieved and cleared, and grateful that Raghav had spoken up for her, though she may still have felt hurt from being kept in.

grounding: A teacher's note on a classmate who quietly spoke up for a child punished for something she did not do.

passage: Arohi, you are still cross about Miss Fernandes, so listen to an old man. I am Kamal, your Nana. When I was ten, my teacher made me stand outside the class for a joke I had not made. I did not talk to her for a month. Then one day she stopped me in the corridor and said, "I was wrong to blame you. I am sorry." My eyes filled. I felt relief, but also a sore spot inside, like a scrape that had not healed. I nodded. Slowly I understood that teachers are people who slip too. When I forgave her, that weight left my chest.

qa.q: Where did the teacher make Kamal stand?
qa.a: She made him stand outside the class.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when his teacher apologised?
qa.a: He felt relieved but also still sore, like a scrape that had not healed.

qa.q: What might Arohi learn from Nana's story about her own anger at Miss Fernandes?
qa.a: She can accept a sincere apology and let herself forgive gently, without pretending it did not hurt, so she does not carry the anger. 🤍

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when she went up to Kamal in the corridor?
qa.a: She was probably uneasy and remorseful, since she had to admit her mistake to a child, and it took courage.

grounding: An elder recalls his teacher admitting she was wrong; he felt relief and a lingering ache, and forgiving gently lifted the anger.

passage: At the school gate, both parents had been called in after a note home about Damini's missing diary. Papa said, "No games this week." Before Damini could explain that the diary was with the librarian, she shouted, "It is not fair! You never listen!" Mama pressed her lips. In the school library, waiting, Damini's friend Lalremsiami whispered, "Cool down first. Then tell them once." Damini looked at the shelves and counted her breaths. Later, at the reading table, she said quietly, "I was upset because I did not get to explain. The diary was with the librarian." Papa sighed. "Show me."

qa.q: Where was the diary really?
qa.a: It was with the librarian.

qa.q: Why did Damini shout at the school gate?
qa.a: She was upset that her parents punished her before hearing her side, and she felt it was not fair.

qa.q: What worked better than shouting for Damini?
qa.a: She cooled down by counting breaths and then told her parents once, calmly, what had happened. 😊

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Damini shouted at the gate?
qa.a: Papa may have felt worried and annoyed at the note, and reacted quickly to the missing diary, then softened when she spoke calmly.

grounding: A child shouts when her parents punish her before hearing her side, then explains calmly once she has cooled down.

passage:
"Mummy, I have to tell you something about my mark sheet."
"What is it, Sangeeta?"
Sangeeta's palms were sweating. She had thought of stuffing the paper into her school bag and saying it had not come. "I got low marks in maths. I was scared to show you."
"Let me see." Gopika read it slowly. "Thank you for telling me at once."
"I made a plan. I will do a page of sums every day and ask Sir to explain fractions again."
"That is a good plan. Shall I sit with you sometimes?"
Sangeeta let out her breath.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta think of doing with the paper before she told her mother?
qa.a: She thought of stuffing it into her school bag and saying it had not come.

qa.q: Why was Sangeeta scared to show the mark sheet?
qa.a: She feared her mother would be disappointed in her, and that fear made her palms sweat.

qa.q: What worked in the way Sangeeta shared her result?
qa.a: She told her mother right away and came with a plan, which kept the fear from growing as it would have if she hid the paper.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt while reading the mark sheet?
qa.a: Gopika probably felt concerned but chose to stay calm and thank her daughter, and to offer help instead of blame.

grounding: A child dreads showing her mark sheet but shares it early with a calm plan, and the fear shrinks.

passage:
"Sharmaji, my son came first in Class 6!" Papa told the man at the gate, and Chaitanya's ears turned red. In the flat, Papa laughed on the phone. Chaitanya sat next to him.
"Papa, I am happy you are happy."
"You should be proud, Chaitanya!"
"I am. But what if I do not get first next time?"
Lalit put down the phone. "You are thinking of the next exam already?"
"A little."
Chaitanya looked at the trophy on the shelf. "I think I am the same me, even if I come third."
Papa was quiet, then nodded.

qa.q: What class did Chaitanya come first in?
qa.a: He came first in Class 6.

qa.q: What worry did Chaitanya have beneath his happiness?
qa.a: He worried about not getting first again next time, feeling pressure to repeat the result.

qa.q: What can Chaitanya do with his happy feelings and the pressure together?
qa.a: He can enjoy his father's joy while reminding himself that he is the same person whatever his rank. 🙂

qa.q: How might Papa see Chaitanya's question?
qa.a: Papa may not have realised his boasting made his son anxious, and he went quiet, showing he was thinking about what Chaitanya said.

grounding: A child enjoys his parents' pride in his marks but feels pressure to repeat it, and reminds himself his worth is more than rank.

passage: On Sunday, the visiting cousin Vishal's report card lay open on the tea table next to Rajni's, and Mummy sighed. "Look, he scored twenty more marks than you in science." Papa shook his head. Rajni's throat tightened. She felt very small in the crowded city flat, with the pressure cooker whistling. She wanted to run into her room. Instead she said, "I know my marks are low. I will try harder. Can you help me with the science chapters after dinner?" Mummy looked surprised, then softer. Vishal quietly pushed the plate of pakoras toward Rajni. Rajni felt her shoulders relax. She was not a number.

qa.q: How many more marks did Vishal score than Rajni in science?
qa.a: He scored twenty more marks than she did.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when her parents compared her to Vishal?
qa.a: She felt small and her throat tightened, and she wanted to run to her room.

qa.q: What could Rajni do if the sighing and comparing happens again?
qa.a: She can say she will try and ask for help, as she did, and remember that her parents' worry is not her fault and does not lower her worth.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt about the comparison?
qa.a: Vishal may have felt awkward at being the yardstick, and his pushing the pakoras toward Rajni suggests he wanted to be kind.

grounding: A child whose parents sigh over her marks and compare her to a cousin says she will try harder and asks for help without losing self-respect.

passage: Friday. Results today. Rituraj came first in the class again, and Ma'am read his name out. I clapped, but my stomach stung like I had swallowed a chilli. I even thought, he just memorises. But I know he does not. On the way home I did not say anything mean, because that would only make me feel worse. At the bus stop I asked, "Rituraj, how did you study for the science test?" He grinned. "I make small question cards and go through them in bed." I am going to make my own cards this weekend. The sting is still there, a little. Kalyani.

qa.q: What does Rituraj make to study for science?
qa.a: He makes small question cards and goes through them in bed.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when Rituraj's name was read out?
qa.a: Kalyani felt envy, which Kalyani describes as a sting in the stomach like a chilli, even while clapping.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that turned envy into something useful?
qa.a: Kalyani asked Rituraj how he studied and planned to make question cards too, instead of running Rituraj down.

qa.q: How might Rituraj have felt when Kalyani asked him how he studied?
qa.a: Rituraj probably felt pleased to be asked and happy to share, and it kept their friendship easy. 😊

grounding: A child feels envy when a friend tops the class and turns it into learning by asking what helped him study.
